dataGaps: Producer support estimate (PSE) or nominal rate of assistance (NRA) by product for Tunisia after 2000: none found. Searches run (web search, November 2026): OECD PSE/agricultural policy monitoring (Tunisia coverage could not be confirmed; OECD pages returned HTTP 403), Ag-Incentives (site returned an empty page), World Bank Distortions to Agricultural Incentives and FAO MAFAP (no Tunisia results). Only cereal NPCs for 1980-1988 (SRC-TG-920) and a 2024 farmgate vs import cost comparison for durum and barley (SRC-TG-705) exist.
World Bank (2006) Tunisia agricultural policy review, the original source of the consumer-cost, GDP and winners/losers simulations: not opened; figures are cited via SRC-TG-710.
Budget transfers to agriculture after 2010 by instrument (price support, input subsidies, investment aid, general services): WTO domestic support notifications after 2014 not opened.
Distribution of support by farm size class (share of transfers going to the largest farms): the claim of regressivity is stated qualitatively by SRC-TG-710 without a quantified distribution.

Status of the Office des Céréales wheat import monopoly after 2016 remains ambiguous: the WTO says it ended in 2016 (SRC-TG-924, para. 4.35); the World Bank in 2024 describes a de jure grain monopoly except barley (SRC-TG-705). The legal text resolving the apparent conflict was not found.

The World Bank wording on beef and milk growth is 'almost one-third (17 percent of the value)' while total agricultural output value grew 67%; 17/67 is about 25%, so the intended denominator is unclear (SRC-TG-710).
Table 9.3 of SRC-TG-710 sums to about 31.7% (2000) and 54.2% (2009) for market price support plus input subsidies, against the text values of 31% and 53% used here.
No sourced projection of how the support structure will evolve (e.g. under an EU DCFTA agricultural chapter).
author: TahaGHZ
excerpt: Tunisian agricultural policy works mainly through guaranteed producer prices for cereals, intervention buying by state offices for milk, sugar beet and tobacco, high tariffs on agri-food imports and fixed consumer…

sections.heading: Problem
sections.content:
Tunisian agricultural policy works mainly through guaranteed producer prices for cereals, intervention buying by state offices for milk, sugar beet and tobacco, high tariffs on agri-food imports and fixed consumer prices and margins (SRC-TG-710, SRC-TG-924). The World Bank calls this "a food security policy" rather than an agricultural policy. In its view the policy pulls land, capital and labour towards continental products (cereals, milk, beef), where Tunisia is not competitive, and away from Mediterranean products (olive oil, fruit, vegetables, dried fruit), where it has a comparative advantage (SRC-TG-710). The direct budget cost was about TND 350 million, or 0.8% of GDP, in 2010 (the report text says 2010, while Table 9.3 gives 350.6 for 2009 and has no 2010 column). Between 2000 and 2009 the share of market price support and input subsidies in agricultural transfers rose from 31% to 53%, while investment aid and general services fell (SRC-TG-710). The support is regressive: it is based on output and farm size, so it mostly benefits large wheat, milk and beef producers. Olive, fruit and vegetable growers in the interior get little support and have difficulty getting finance (SRC-TG-710).

**Correction to the framing we were given.** The research brief asked whether administered prices impose negative support on farmers. The evidence says the sign has changed over time and, for cereals, varies with world prices. Before 1986, prices were fixed below world levels and agriculture was implicitly taxed (SRC-TG-920). From 1987, cereal producer prices were pushed above world prices (NPC 1.37 for durum in late 1987) (SRC-TG-920), and wheat remained "overprotected" in 1995 (SRC-TG-921). The 2014 analysis, using 2000s data, describes support, not taxation, for cereals, milk and beef (SRC-TG-710). After the 2021-2022 world price rise the sign flipped again for cereals. The World Bank wrote in 2024 that decreed farmgate prices "have been below import-parity prices". Even after increases of about 61-64% between 2021 and 2023, February 2024 farmgate prices for durum wheat and barley were 3% and 14% below the OC import cost (SRC-TG-705). Because the decreed price is fixed for a season while world prices move, cereal growers are subsidised in some years and implicitly taxed in others (see FND-TG-702). Over the 2000s, when evidence exists across products, the problem was mainly how support was distributed (by product, farm size and region) and how it was delivered (price support instead of investment and services), not a net tax on farmers. Whether that still holds after 2021 cannot be shown without a PSE/NRA series. Mediterranean products are disadvantaged relatively, because protection pulls resources into continental products (SRC-TG-710). This record found no sourced estimate of whether Mediterranean products are taxed in absolute terms (see data_gaps).

sections.heading: Root causes
sections.content:
1. **Self-sufficiency in staples as the policy goal (legacy).** The state cereal system set up in the 1960s-70s is covered in FND-TG-702. The PASA reforms of 1986-1995 cut input subsidies but kept administered wheat prices and the offices' marketing role (FND-TG-920, SRC-TG-921). The guaranteed-price and state-trading structure in place in 2016 is the result (SRC-TG-924).
2. **Output-based and area-based support.** Because support is based on output and farm size, it goes mostly to a few large landowners. The World Bank says this contradicts the common belief in Tunisia that the policy protects small family farms (SRC-TG-710).
3. **State trading and price controls.** The Office des Céréales held the wheat import monopoly until 2016 under the WTO account; the World Bank later described a de jure grain monopoly except barley (SRC-TG-924, SRC-TG-705). The OCT imported sugar in a de facto monopoly according to Tunisia's 2006 state-trading notification (SRC-TG-924, para. 3.168). The state fixed consumer prices for bread, flour, couscous, oil, sugar, milk and tea, and margins for rice, poultry, eggs and many fruits and vegetables (SRC-TG-924). The ONH guarantees a minimum price to olive oil producers who cannot sell (SRC-TG-924).
4. **Drift back towards distorting instruments.** Tunisia committed at the Uruguay Round (1994) to reduce domestic support from USD 76 million to 66 million, yet agricultural support spending rose steadily over the 2000s (SRC-TG-710). After PASA removed fertiliser and feed subsidies (FND-TG-920), input subsidies, mainly fuel, milk collection premia and irrigation, made up 20-25% of transfers by 2008-2009 (SRC-TG-710).

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.content:
- Market price support is over 30% of budget transfers. Milk takes over 50% of price support spending and cereals about a third (SRC-TG-710, p. 265).
- Input subsidies are 20-25% of transfers. In 2008-09 they went about 40% to fuel, 40% to milk collection premia and 18% to irrigation (SRC-TG-710, p. 266).
- Average MFN tariff on agri-food is 24.6%, against 16.5% for all products. 60.5% of agricultural tariff lines exceed 15% (SRC-TG-710, p. 266).
- Budget cost was reported as TND 350 million (0.8% of GDP) in 2010; Table 9.3 gives TND 350.6 million for 2009 and has no 2010 column. The share of price support and input subsidies rose from 31% (2000) to 53% (2009) (SRC-TG-710, p. 266).
- Agricultural output grew 67% in value over 1990-2010. The source says "almost one-third (17 percent of the value)" came from beef and milk; 17/67 is about 25%, so the denominator is ambiguous (SRC-TG-710, p. 265).
- Consumer subsidies for cereals rose from TND 170 million (2004) to TND 1,360 million (2014) according to the WTO text (SRC-TG-924, para. 4.34). The same report's Table 3.20 gives cereals and derivatives at TND 170.9 million (2005), 1,152.4 million (2014) and 1,359.3 million (2015), so the source is internally inconsistent on the 2014 value; roughly TND 1.2-1.4 billion in 2014-15.
- Model estimates from World Bank (2006), cited in 2014. Agricultural trade protection costs consumers 4-5.6% of spending. Removing tariffs would raise GDP by about 0.8% but shift about 87,000 agricultural jobs to other sectors. About 70% of farms would gain from removing price distortions, mostly olive, fruit, vegetable and sheep farms in the centre and south. Losers would be cereal farms in the north and north-west (SRC-TG-710, pp. 267-268). These are counterfactual simulations, not measurements.

**Counter-view.** Boughzala and Elloumi (1992) found, with a risk-constrained farm model, that full liberalisation was not in Tunisia's interest while the EEC protected and subsidised its own agriculture. They found Tunisia would gain only if major producers also liberalised (SRC-TG-922). The 2014 World Bank simulation includes a scenario without EU subsidies that still shows gains (SRC-TG-710), but the two studies use different models and periods. This record does not settle the disagreement.

**Source conflict.** The WTO Secretariat, citing Tunisia's 2006 state-trading notification, lists the Office des Céréales as wheat and barley import monopolist. In its 2016 update it says the OC held the wheat import monopoly until 2016, with wheat duties cut to zero from January 2016 (SRC-TG-924). The World Bank in 2024 describes the OC as holding a de jure monopoly over grain trade, domestic collection and imports, except barley, opened to selected private operators for imports since April 2023 (SRC-TG-705). All three statements are recorded.

sections.heading: Why confidence is what it is
sections.content: Medium. The description of instruments (administered prices, state monopolies, price controls) is consistent across the World Bank and the WTO Secretariat (SRC-TG-710, SRC-TG-924). The diagnosis of bias and regressivity rests mainly on one institution, the World Bank, which has advocated liberalisation since 1986. Its quantitative impacts are model simulations from a 2006 study we could not open. Budget data stop at 2010 and WTO data at 2016, so whether the structure still holds in 2026 is assumed, not shown (trend: unknown). Apart from the 2024 cereal price comparison (SRC-TG-705), no PSE/NRA series was found to quantify support by product (see data_gaps).

sections.heading: Links to other sectors
sections.content:
- **Energy.** Fuel subsidies were about 40% of agricultural input subsidies in 2008-09 (SRC-TG-710). Agricultural support therefore depends partly on energy pricing policy (energy lane, theme energy-subsidies).
- **Water.** Irrigation subsidies were about 18% of input subsidies in 2008-09 (SRC-TG-710). Protection of irrigated milk and beef production shapes demand for irrigation water. This record does not quantify the water used by protected products.
- **Agriculture (other findings).** Cereal-specific pricing and the subsidy system are in FND-TG-702, import dependence in FND-TG-700. Lack of finance for Mediterranean crops is in FND-TG-922.

sections.heading: Leads for phase 2
sections.content:
- Shift from price support to decoupled direct income payments, as proposed by the World Bank (SRC-TG-710, recommendations section; compared to the EU CAP reforms since the mid-1990s).
- Horizontal support (finance, risk management, extension, land market) instead of product-specific support (SRC-TG-710).
- Fuller use of EU preferential export quotas for olive oil, citrus and tomatoes (SRC-TG-710).
- Zero wheat import duty from January 2016 (SRC-TG-924, para. 4.35).
- Investment incentives code and Decree n° 94-427 of 14 February 1994 on agricultural investment grants (SRC-TG-924, para. 4.13).
- ONH minimum price guarantee for olive oil (SRC-TG-924, para. 4.48).

sections.heading: Verification
sections.content:
Claims were traced to the World Bank 2014 report chapter 9 (SRC-TG-710), the WTO Trade Policy Review of 2016 (SRC-TG-924), the World Bank grain note of March 2024 (SRC-TG-705) and the Persee copy of SRC-TG-922.

**Independent review, 21 November 2026:** pass after corrections. Checked: SRC-TG-710 pp. 264-267 and 277 (0.8% of GDP and TND 350 million, Table 9.3, 31 to 53%, milk over 50%, 24.6% tariff, 17% of value, 4 to 5.6% consumer cost, 76 to 66 million USD commitment, input-subsidy split, 70% of farms gain, losers are cereal farms in the north and north-west, little support and difficult finance for interior Mediterranean crops; the last two passages were located by me in the original after the reviewer could not find them); SRC-TG-924 paras. 3.168, 4.34, 4.35, 4.48 and Table 3.20; SRC-TG-705 footnote 3 and Box 1; SRC-TG-922 résumé p. 74. Corrections: sugar monopoly "within its tariff quota" replaced by the source's "de facto monopoly"; cereal subsidy figures now give both the text and Table 3.20 values; Table 9.3 arithmetic noted as a data gap. Independent teammate sign-off is outstanding; reviewer and author share the TahaGHZ identity, so the record is not validated.

resolvedSources.extracts:
Dated March 1, 2024. Sectoral context, para 8, p. 3:

> For the fourth consecutive year, below-average rainfall and extreme heat have combined to dramatically compromise Tunisia's grain production in 2022/23. As shown in Table 1 below, the Grain Board collected less than half of durum wheat quantities in 2023 compared to average drought years 2020-22 and two-thirds less than in a non-drought year (such as 2019), and almost no barley (1.3 percent of average drought years).

Table 1, "Grain quantities collected by OC (2019-2023)", '000 t, source Tunisia Grain Board (OC), rows (2019 / average 2020-2022 / 2023):

> Durum wheat 876.4 685.6 286.7
> Soft wheat 75.4 31.3 6.2
> Barley 332.9 39.5 0.5
> Total 1284.7 756.4 293.4

Para 8, p. 3 (continued):

> Consequently, average monthly grain import needs have skyrocketed (100,000 MT/month for durum wheat and 100,000 MT/month for barley, currently estimated at US$48 million/month for durum wheat and US$28 million/month for barley).

Footnote 15:

> This is particularly true in Tunisia where people remember vividly the bread riots that occurred from December 1983 to January 1984, triggered by a temporary rise in the price of bread due to the government austerity program.

Para 9, p. 3:

> For the period from July 2023 to June 2024, the Grain Board is facing an additional financing gap of around US$522 million due to very low local harvest of durum wheat and barley.

Footnote to Table 2, p. 4:

> Soft wheat import needs are not substantially impacted by drought since Tunisia is 95 percent dependent on imports.

Box 1, p. 4:

> The Grain Board (OC) is an SOE created in 1962 under the tutelage of Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries (MAWRF) with a core mandate to regulate and ensure a stable supply of grain on the domestic market through domestic grain harvest collection, imports, and the management of strategic reserves.

> The OC has a de jure monopoly over grain trade (domestic collection and imports), except for barley (animal feed) for which domestic collection (traditionally) and imports (since April 2023) have been authorized for selected private operators.

> The OC buys grain domestically at farmgate prices fixed annually by a government decree. These prices have been below import-parity prices; they were increased by around 60 percent since 2022 to incentivize production.

> The OC sells the grain it purchases at subsidized prices to the millers who are granted specific acquisition quotas; the millers in turn sell the milled products (soft wheat bread flour, soft wheat pastry flour, durum semolina) to bakeries and processors similarly at subsidized prices under quota assignments. End products (such as bread, pasta, and couscous) are sold to consumers at subsidized prices.

> Because of CGC protracted payments, OC must resort to financing by the National Agriculture Bank which is difficult to mobilize and costly.

> CGC, a state-owned entity created in 1970, is responsible for providing compensatory payments to operators at the different segments of the grain value chain to cover the gap between market and administered prices.

Footnote 3:

> Farmgate gate prices in 2023 have been increased by 60.9 percent, 64.2 percent and 60.7 percent for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley respectively, compared to 2021. In February 2024, official farmgate prices for durum wheat and barley are respectively 3 percent sand 14 percent lower than OC import cost (Source OC).

Box 1 continued, p. 5:

> (iii) there are illegal and improper use of subsidized grain products, i.e., improper use of semolina for feed to animals, illegal leakages of grain products towards neighboring countries, as well as excessive consumption and wastage of bread and wheat-based products by end-consumers, e.g., wastage of 900,000 "baguettes" daily; and (iv) the system limits the active participation of the private sector

Para 10, p. 5:

> For calendar years 2022 and 2023, the OC was supposed to receive TND6,625 million (Tunisian Dinar) – i.e., approximately US$2,106 million - from the CGC, but funding effectively received from the compensation fund was only 38 percent (i.e., TND2,543 million or US$808 million).

> As of February 2024, the OC's estimated overall 2023 balance (yet to be audited) amounts to TND -900 million (equivalent to US$ -286 million) and OC's total debt to commercial banks is TND6,343 million (equivalent to US$2,016 million, out of which 83 percent towards the National Agriculture Bank - BNA).

Para 11, p. 5:

> the GoT is carrying out a series of measures that, if fully implemented, would lead to a more sustainable sector and sizeable budget savings in the range of US$400-600 million per year.

Para 10, p. 5 (continued):

> This situation makes it very difficult for OC to access additional financing from commercial banks for grain imports

Para 13:

> This series of reforms would lead to OC's budget and fiscal savings estimated at US$576 million per year

Table 3, "Summary reform measures of the grain value chain and associated savings", measure names (rows extracted as text; fiscal columns not used):

> 4 Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC) [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 5 Improved access to seasonal credit for grain producers [...] Approved (2024 Fiscal Law)- December 31, 2023
> 9 Liberalization of soft wheat imports for industrial processing of pastry flour (PS-7) [...] Planned: Cabinet Council to review the draft Decision

Footnote 4 (to Table 3 measure "Strengthening of compensation for losses (FIDAC)", approved in the 2024 Fiscal Law):

> FIDAC (Fonds d'Indemnisation des Dommages Agricoles causés par les Calamités naturelles): is a farmers' compensation fund in case of natural disaster, including drought.

Results framework, p. 43:

> Food subsidy reform implementation plan prepared [...] Preparation of a reform plan for food subsidies and switch to cash transfer, including consultation and communication.

Footnote 17:

> 43.3 percent of bread subsidy for "Gros pain" and 43.5 percent of subsidy for other staple durum wheat-based products go to the poorest two quintiles of Tunisia households in 2022.

> Taking action to improve access to finance for the agricultural sector. Access to finance is especially challenging for investments in arboriculture (olive oil and fruit), which entail several years between the initial investment and the start of the production phase.
resolvedSources.notes: Chapter of the World Bank Development Policy Review published in 2014; underlying analyses date from 2006-2012 (CGE model World Bank 2006; DRC analysis World Bank 2009 using 2000, 2004, 2008 prices). Its view that cereal producers receive market price support contrasts with the 2024 World Bank statement that farmgate prices were below import parity (SRC-TG-705); the two describe different periods and price contexts. The DRC table extracted with shifted values and is not quoted; only prose is used.

resolvedSources.title: Tunisia - Agricultural Sector Adjustment Loan (Loan 2754-TUN), Project Completion Report (Report No. 9308)
resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank, Agricultural Operations Division, Country Department II, EMENA Region
resolvedSources.extracts:
Para. 1.05 (situation before the 1986 programme):

> Within the agricultural sector itself, there were a number of constraints to development. Negative protection rates and worsening terms of trade with other sectors, particularly industry, made agriculture and related support services unattractive for new private direct investment. [...] Support services were controlled to a large degree by the Government. These operations were often inefficient, wasting resources for the economy at large, and frequently resulting in interruptions of supply to farmers.

Para. 6.11 (prices and incentives framework):

> At the time the loan was developed, prices of both agricultural outputs and inputs (fertilizers, improved seed, herbicides and livestock feed) were below world prices and fixed on the basis of a cost-plus methodology. The medium-term program called for linkage with world market prices to be achieved by the end of the medium-term program (1991)

Para. 6.12:

> Output prices for durum wheat, bread wheat and barley were raised by 12.6%, 3.5% and 6.3% in real terms respectively for the 1987 crop year and by 8.3%, 6.7% and 11.4% in real terms respectively for the 1988 crop year. Nominal protection coefficients rose from .89, .98 and .82 for durum, bread wheat and barley respectively between 1980 and 1985 to 1.04, 1.03 and .90 in 1988

Para. 6.13:

> Nominal protection coefficients comparing producer prices to actual world prices were extremely high due to plummeting values for basic grains on the world markets (NPCs were 1.37, 1.27 and 1.29 for durum, bread wheat and barley respectively). [...] At the time, the Tunisians were more concerned about creating incentives for agricultural production than about the budgetary costs of further price increases.

Para. 6.14:

> It was not foreseen at the time that a situation of implicit taxation of the agricultural sector could become one of over-protection.

Para. 6.15:

> Increases in input prices were suspended for the 1989 season due to the severe drought in 1988 [...] Under ASAL-II the Government expects to resume input price increases for the 1990 season and to gradually eliminate all of the input subsidies by 1992.
resolvedSources.notes: Bank self-evaluation of its own loan (ASAL I, approved 1986). Para. 6.12 reports NPCs rising from .89/.98/.82 in 1980-85 to 1.04/1.03/.90 in 1988, but Annex 2 Table 1 shows the bases differ: early 1980s ratios are Actual/Import-equivalent; the formula row begins in 1986/87. Only the 1988 leg is against the moving-average formula. Para. 6.13 compares producer prices to actual world prices of late 1987. These series answer different questions and must not be mixed. The text file is OCR from a scanned original; obvious OCR errors (e.g. "Withie", "resoucces") are corrected above. Cereals-only NPCs; no aggregate PSE/NRA for all agriculture is given.

resolvedSources.title: Republic of Tunisia - Agriculture Sector Adjustment Loan II (Loan 3078-TUN), Implementation Completion Report (Report No. 15355)
resolvedSources.publisher: World Bank, Natural Resources and Environment Division, Maghreb and Iran Department, MENA Region
resolvedSources.extracts:
Executive summary, para. iii (reform areas of the Medium-Term Agricultural Sector Adjustment Programme, MTASAP):

> parastatal reforms: divestiture to the private sector of numerous activities of the Cereals Marketing Board (OC), the National Edible Oil Board (ONH) and the Livestock and Pastures Board (OEP) [...] pricing and marketing: adjustment of prices for cereals and milk to keep them more closely aligned with world prices, the introduction of more market driven prices for beef, the reduction of input subsidies, and the liberalization of meat and milk imports

Para. v:

> an analysis prepared by the Bank before appraisal [...] made it clear that the fiscal balance and sector efficiency measures sought under the ASAL II would result in marginally negative sector growth and incomes for farmers. The President's Report did not present these results because of concern that doing so would weaken the support of the key constituency for the Loan, the Ministry of Agriculture (MOA)

Para. vi:

> The Loan achieved its fiscal objectives since budget costs of subsidies for inputs and credit were substantially reduced -- from 73 to 15 million DT for inputs financed through the General Compensation Fund, through a 40 percent real increase in irrigation tariffs, and a reduction by two-thirds of budget allocations to finance rural credit subsidies [...] Parastatal reform was generally successful in disengaging the organizations from non-core activities, but much less so in achieving greater efficiency through increasing competition from the private sector on a more level playing field, particularly for domestic cereals collection and beef imports [...] wheats continue to be overprotected by restrictive import policy.

Para. 13 (cereals collection):

> in practice very little progress is evident in transferring cereals collection to the private sector. Only three new private participants in cereals collection have emerged, and their activities have remained limited. Risks remain large as long as the OC retains both its role a direct competitor in grain collection and also regulator of the effort to promote private collection.

Para. 15:

> Administered producer prices for soft and hard wheat remained high compared with the agreed formula, while barley producer prices have tracked the formula more closely.

Para. 26:

> The inputs involved were fertilizers, animal feeds, improved cereals seeds, seed potatoes and the herbicide 2-4-D. This objective was fully met, with subsidies either substantially reduced or eliminated. The CGC is the financing mechanism for these subsidies, which peaked at DT 73 million in the drought of 1989 but fell below DT 15 million by 1993.

Para. 27:

> Subsidies for three of the four principal types of fertilizer used in Tunisia have been eliminated. Subsidy reduction began with freeing distribution margins with the 1987/88 campaign, and since 1991 by removal of remaining product subsidies (1991 for Super 16, 1992 for Ammonitre 33, and 1993 for DAP). Only Super 45, which accounts for roughly one-quarter of the total quantities of fertilizer applied, still benefits from a (declining) subsidy. [...] For the 1986-92 period, the increase in real prices of fertilizers averaged 6% annually.

Para. 28:

> Overall subsidies for animal feed peaked in the drought of 1989 at 49 million dinar (current prices) before falling to 4 million dinars in 1992-93.

Para. 13 (continued):

> Transfer of OC facilities to the private sector has proved to be unsuccessful because of the lack of interest linked to a condition in the cahier de charges requiring that all existing personnel be maintained by new management.

Para. 16:

> It eliminated the subsidy for transport cost equalization for cereals, and regarding storage, the Government tested, then implemented an approach for private storage, with the introduction of monthly payments for private storage intended to simulate average seasonal price movements. In conjunction with investment incentives, the promotion of private storage of cereals has proven successful

Para. 18 (olive oil):

> new legislation was passed in 1994 that brought much more extensive liberalization to olive oil exports. [...] Nevertheless, the exporters remain concerned about the ambiguous position of the ONH's which mixes elements of partnership, through provision of services and private sector support, and competition, largely through the ONH's own exports to the European market

Paras. 19-20 (milk):

> a condition of effectiveness was elimination of quantitative restrictions on imports of powdered milk and imposition of a variable levy necessary to provide 15% nominal protection according to an agreed moving average formula. [...] The variable levy was implemented in 1990, and subsequently revised in 1991 and 1993. No adjustments have occurred in the variable levy, or in producer support prices, since 1993.

Para. 23 (beef):

> El Louhoum still accounts for about half of beef imports. [...] In 1994 it was obliged to purchase all live cattle presented to it at a fixed price. El Louhoum continues to benefit from subsidies, does not pay the variable levy on meat imports that the private sector is obliged to pay, and sells its products into its own retail structure with prices that are administratively fixed.

Para. 28 (continued):

> This consisted almost entirely of subsidies on barley, as subsidies on corn were eliminated in 1992 and those on soybean meal in 1993.

Para. 28 (drought feed policy):

> Barley is used to compensate pastoralists for grazing land that is taken out of use during rehabilitation programs, and also small livestock farmers during drought years with the intention of maintaining herd sizes and stabilizing incomes. Corn and soybean meal benefit poultry raisers and also dairy operations, mostly on larger scale farms.

English gloss: the report describes subsidised barley as drought support intended to maintain smallholder herds and compensate pastoralists; corn and soybean meal are used by poultry and dairy, especially larger farms.

Para. 31 (irrigation tariffs):

> The tariffs vary by Region, but averaged 41 millimes /m3 in 1993. This is about 75 percent of the costs of operations and maintenance in the old MOA definition, which does not yet include amortisation and provisioning for repair of civil works and equipment within the perimeter, and about 63 percent of operations and maintenance costs which include these latter components.

Para. 59:

> The sustainability of these subsidy reductions does not seem in doubt: there was no backtracking on the reductions during the subsequent droughts in 1994 and 1995.

Para. 62 (updated multi-market model):

> the realized price policy changes alone would have decreased value added by 1.3 percent [...] there was a small decline, under 1 percent per annum, in real incomes, with the exception of the low income group in the north and center of the country, for whom incomes increased.

Para. 63:

> The DGPDIA has analyzed income trends for four typical farm types ranging from 5 to 80 hectares during the adjustment period. [...] Net incomes derived from the models are stagnant at best for the smaller farm types, and decline for the largest representative farm from 1989 levels.
resolvedSources.notes: Bank self-evaluation, covering 1989-1995. Para. 60 admits monitoring data were largely not collected, so income effects rest on a model and on four representative farm budgets, not on observed household incomes. OCR from scanned original; spelling errors corrected in extracts.

resolvedSources.title: Libéralisation de la politique agricole en Tunisie et la réforme de la PAC
resolvedSources.publisher: Économie rurale, n° 211, pp. 74-79 (Persée), authors Mongi Boughzala and Mohamed Elloumi
resolvedSources.extracts:
Résumé, p. 74:

> A l'aide d'un modèle de programmation linéaire qui intègre la contrainte risque, nous avons pu démontrer que la Tunisie n'a pas intérêt, dans la conjoncture actuelle, à libéraliser totalement sa politique agricole. Par contre, dans le cas d'une libéralisation réelle des échanges au niveau mondial, la Tunisie gagnerait à libéraliser largement son économie agricole.

English gloss: using a risk-constrained linear programming model, the authors find that Tunisia had no interest, under the conditions of the time, in fully liberalising its agricultural policy; if world trade were really liberalised, Tunisia would gain from liberalising widely.

Introduction, p. 74:

> suite aux pressions des institutions financières internationales, la Tunisie a été amenée à adopter, à partir de la fin de l'année 1986, un Plan d'Ajustement Structurel qui donne une large place dans les réformes au secteur agricole (PASA). Toutefois la libéralisation, entreprise dans le cadre du PASA, reste timide et connaît des lenteurs qui sont dues à la fois aux résistances internes, aux conditions réelles sur les marchés internationaux et à la politique protectionniste de nos principaux partenaires commerciaux.

English gloss: following pressure from international financial institutions, Tunisia adopted from late 1986 a structural adjustment plan with a large agricultural component (PASA). The liberalisation under PASA remained timid and slow because of internal resistance, actual conditions on world markets and the protectionism of Tunisia's main trading partners.

p. 75:

> Ces mesures concernent les prix, les subventions à la production et à la consommation, la libéralisation des circuits de commercialisation et de collecte etc.. Ce plan a pour objectif principal le renforcement des mécanismes de marché et le désengagement de l'Etat des fonctions de production et de commercialisation. Il comprend deux volets, d'un côté une valorisation des prix à la production pour atteindre les prix internationaux (non subventionnés) en gardant en plus une légère protection pour les produits dits stratégiques ; d'un autre côté, il est prévu à la fois une plus grande libéralisation de la commercialisation à l'amont et à l'aval de la production et surtout une réduction progressive des subventions à la production.

English gloss: PASA measures covered prices, production and consumption subsidies and the liberalisation of marketing and collection; its aim was to strengthen market mechanisms and withdraw the state from production and marketing; producer prices were to be raised to (unsubsidised) world levels with a slight protection for "strategic" products, and production subsidies were to be phased out.

p. 75:

> L'agriculture [...] occupe près de 26 % de la population active totale. [...] Elle contribue aussi pour 14 % au PIB.

English gloss: agriculture employed about 26% of the labour force and contributed 14% of GDP (early 1990s).
resolvedSources.notes: Short conference paper (CIHEAM/IAM-M session, November 1991). Useful as an academic Tunisian counter-view to the World Bank's liberalisation case. The model results are summarised, not fully documented in the 6 pages.

resolvedSources.title: Examen des politiques commerciales - Rapport du Secrétariat - Tunisie (WT/TPR/S/341)
resolvedSources.extracts:
Para. 3.167-3.169:

> La dernière notification de la Tunisie à l'OMC en matière de commerce d'État au sens de l'article XVII du GATT date de 2006. Elle indique la présence de neuf entreprises commerciales d'État. En 2004, 16% des importations tunisiennes était le fait d'entreprises commerciales d'État. Il n'a pas été possible d'obtenir une estimation de la part correspondante en 2015.
>
> Selon cette notification, l'Office du commerce de Tunisie (OCT) importe du sucre (en monopole de fait) et, sans droits exclusifs, le thé (noir et vert), le café vert et certains "produits conjoncturels" (principalement des pommes de terre et du riz), et procède à leur distribution en gros.
>
> L'Office des céréales exerce le monopole d'importation du blé dur, du blé tendre, et de l'orge. [...] L'Office national des huiles (ONH) importe des huiles de graines (soja, colza, olive) et exporte de l'huile d'olive, sans droits exclusifs

English gloss: Tunisia's last GATT Article XVII state-trading notification dates from 2006 and lists nine state trading enterprises; in 2004 they accounted for 16% of Tunisian imports. According to that notification, OCT imports sugar (de facto monopoly) and, without exclusive rights, tea, green coffee and some "conjunctural products" (mainly potatoes and rice). The Cereals Office holds the import monopoly for durum wheat, soft wheat and barley. ONH imports seed oils and exports olive oil without exclusive rights.

Para. 4.32-4.33:

> De nombreuses entreprises publiques continuent de concurrencer le secteur privé dans la production et le commerce agroalimentaire; certaines ont des positions exclusives dans la commercialisation, y compris à l'importation et à l'exportation. [...] L'État tunisien continue d'intervenir dans le secteur agroalimentaire en fixant les prix à la consommation (par exemple pain, farine, couscous, huile, sucre, lait et thé); le prix de revient industriel (par exemple sel, levure, café, bière); ou les marges de distribution (riz, volaille, oeufs, nombreux fruits et légumes et préparations alimentaires, tableau 3.20).

English gloss: many state enterprises still compete with the private sector in agri-food production and trade, some with exclusive marketing positions including import and export. The state still fixes consumer prices (bread, flour, couscous, oil, sugar, milk, tea), industrial cost prices, or distribution margins (rice, poultry, eggs, many fruits and vegetables).

Para. 4.34:

> l'Office des céréales est chargé d'acheter, sur le marché local, le blé dur et le blé tendre à des prix fixés par l'État. [...] Les charges liées au subventionnement par les pouvoirs publics des prix à la consommation pour les seules céréales s'élevaient à 170 millions de dinars en 2004; elles sont passées à 1 360 millions de dinars (plus de 600 millions d'euros) en 2014.

English gloss: the Cereals Office buys local durum and soft wheat at state-fixed prices. Consumer price subsidies for cereals alone rose from TND 170 million (2004) to TND 1,360 million (2014).

Para. 4.35:

> L'Office des céréales disposait jusqu'en 2016 du monopole d'importation du blé dur et tendre [...] Depuis janvier 2016, le droit de douane a été réduit à zéro sur les importations de blé. Selon les autorités, les importations de blé hors-contingent par le secteur privé sont désormais à taux zéro.

English gloss: the Cereals Office held the durum and soft wheat import monopoly until 2016; since January 2016 the wheat import duty is zero and, according to the authorities, out-of-quota private imports are now duty-free.

Para. 4.41:

> L'Office du commerce détient encore le monopole de l'importation au sein de ce CT, et délivre les autorisations d'importation de sucre.

English gloss: OCT still holds the import monopoly within the sugar tariff quota and issues sugar import authorisations.

Para. 4.48:

> L'ONH garantit un prix minimum aux producteurs qui, pour une raison ou une autre, n'ont pu avoir une meilleure offre pour écouler leur production. L'ONH achète cependant l'huile d'olive auprès des producteurs à un prix librement négocié.

English gloss: ONH guarantees a minimum price to producers who could not get a better offer for their output; ONH otherwise buys olive oil from producers at freely negotiated prices.

Para. 4.12:

> La dernière notification de la Tunisie à l'OMC en matière de soutien interne porte sur 2014.
resolvedSources.notes: Secretariat report, written in French, for Tunisia's third trade policy review. Paras. 3.168-3.169 describe the 2006 state-trading notification ("Selon cette notification"), so the present tense there reflects 2006; para. 4.35 updates this to 2016 (monopoly held "until 2016"). The apparent contradiction is a difference of reference date. Gives no PSE/NRA estimate.

relatedItems.title: The state cereal system (Office des Céréales monopoly, decreed prices, CGC subsidies) built in 1962-1971 now strains public finances and blunts market signals
Tunisia imports more than half of its cereals (about 60% on ITES averages) and almost all of its soft (bread) wheat, even in good harvest years
The 1986-1995 agricultural adjustment programme (PASA) removed most input subsidies but left administered wheat prices and the state offices' dual role in place
In a 2012 World Bank study, fewer than one farmer in ten borrowed from banks while about a quarter were barred by old arrears; repeated debt write-offs since 1999 have not broken the cycle

Irrigated fresh tomatoes, watermelons and citrus are grown almost entirely for the home market (about 2.4-4.1% exported in 2022), and agricultural policy as assessed by the World Bank in 2014 was biased against exports, so export promotion is not the main driver of their water use

Tunisian livestock runs on imported feed: all maize and soybeans and, in drought years, most barley come from abroad, so feed for livestock is priced on world markets and exposed to the dinar and to import disruptions

The dairy sector built in the 1990s on imported Holstein cows and imported concentrates is contracting: milk output fell about 16% from its 2021 peak to 2025 and the estimated herd shrinks about 2.5% a year (no census since 2019) after drought and feed price shocks; the ministry and farmers describe a lasting gap between feed costs and the administered milk price, frozen at 1,340 millimes since late 2022 or early 2023
